thread.title: Powell signals he’s flexible on interest rates but not resigning if Trump asks

author: Greg Robb
title: Powell signals he’s flexible on interest rates but not resigning if Trump asks
text:
Reuters Fed Chairman Jerome Powell, former Fed chairs Janet Yellen and Ben Bernanke (R) speak during a panel discussion at the American Economic Association meeting in Atlanta. Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell said Friday he’s flexible about future monetary policy moves but inflexible about completing his four-year term at the helm of the U.S. central bank.
In a moderated discussion at the American Economics Association meeting in Atlanta, Powell said he would not resign if asked by President Donald Trump. The president has frequently criticized Powell in interviews and tweets, leading to a debate about whether he might try to force the Fed chairman out.
Related: Why Trump can’t fire Powell for disagreement over monetary policy
In his remarks about the economy and monetary policy, Powell stressed to uneasy financial markets that the central bank wasn’t going to push interest rates higher or shrink the balance sheet regardless of the cost.
Monetary policy “was not on a preset course”
“We will be patient as we watch to see how the economy evolves,” given the low inflation outlook, he said.
The central bank is prepared to shift course “significantly” if necessary.
“We will be prepared to adjust policy quickly and flexibility and to use all our tools to support the economy should that be appropriate,” Powell said.
Financial markets, notably the S&P 500 index SPX, +3.55% have plummeted over fears the Fed intended to move into “restrictive” territory or deliberately slow the economy down. Stocks rallied on Friday, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA, +3.53% jumping more than 700 points at the peak.
Powell said the Fed was alert that financial markets were signaling concern about downside risks to the economy. But he pushed back on the pessimism, saying the “hard” economic data, including the jobs report released earlier Friday, signaled continued economic momentum into 2019.
Read: U.S. gains 312,000 jobs in 10-month high that shattered Wall Street forecasts
The chairman specifically stressed that this flexibility included the runoff of the Fed’s balance sheet. At a press conference last month, Powell had said that process was on autopilot.
The central banker also played down investor concerns about China’s economy that spiked after Apple Inc. AAPL, +3.88% cut its revenue forecast late Wednesday, citing weakness in the country’s economy. Powell said he expected growth to continue this year in China.
The Fed will take a “risk management” approach to policy decisions in coming months, Powell said.
The Fed has penciled in two rate increases this year. Investors think it is likely that rates don’t move higher in 2019.
Ward McCarthy, chief financial economist, at Jefferies, said Powell took rate increases off the table in January and March.
“The [Federal Open Market Committee] is not done raising rates, but…is not going to raise rates at a time when inflation will be falling below target and financial conditions are tightening,” McCarthy wrote in a Friday note to clients.
J.P. Morgan economists lowered their expectations of rate hikes.
"Powell’s message was unmistakable, in our opinion, and we now look for only two hikes this year, in July and December. " - JPMorgan
